blocks.text: Sometimes you just want to poke at an MCP server. You do not want to write a client, import an SDK, or open an editor.
A command line tool lets you do exactly that. You type a command, the tool talks to the server, and you see the result right there in your terminal.
This lesson walks through what these CLI tools do, the common commands you will reach for, and when a CLI is enough versus when you need a real client.
1. What an MCP CLI Tool Is

blocks.alt: What an MCP CLI Tool Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450487-695086830.png
An MCP CLI tool is a small program you run from a terminal that speaks the MCP protocol on your behalf.
It starts or connects to a server, sends a JSON RPC request, and prints back whatever the server replies with.
You never see the JSON RPC messages themselves. The tool hides all of that behind plain commands and flags.

items: No client code to write or maintain
No editor or IDE required, just a terminal
Fast to run once and throw away
Easy to drop into a shell script or a pipeline

blocks.text: 2. Why Skip Writing a Client
Writing even a small MCP client means picking an SDK, setting up a project, and wiring a transport before you can call a single tool.
That is fine when a client is the actual deliverable. It is a lot of ceremony when all you want is to check one thing.
A CLI tool collapses that whole setup into a single command you can run in seconds.
3. Popular CLI Tools for MCP
A few different tools cover this space, and most teams end up using more than one depending on the task.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tool","What it is good for"],"rows":[["MCP Inspector CLI mode","Scripted calls against a server using the same tool used for visual debugging"],["mcptools","A dedicated command line client with short commands for tools, resources, and prompts"],["Custom shell wrapper","A thin script around any SDK client for a very specific repeated check"]]}

blocks.text: This lesson mostly uses the Inspector in its CLI mode, since it ships with the protocol tooling and needs no extra install.
4. Installing a CLI Tool
Most of these tools are npm packages, so npx is the fastest way to try one without a permanent install.

code.content:
# run the Inspector in CLI mode, no install needed
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method tools/list

# or install a dedicated CLI globally
npm install -g mcptools

blocks.text: Global install is worth it once you use a tool daily. Otherwise npx keeps your machine clean.
5. Connecting to a Server from the CLI

blocks.alt: Connecting to a Server from the CLI
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450488-427921814.png
A CLI tool needs to know how to reach your server, and that means telling it the transport and the command or URL to use.

code.content:
# stdio transport, the CLI spawns your server as a subprocess
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method tools/list

# http transport, the CLI connects to a running server
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli --url http://localhost:3000/mcp --method tools/list

blocks.text: Stdio is common for local development. Http fits a server that is already running somewhere, local or remote.
6. Listing Available Tools
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450488-996690409.png
The very first thing worth running against any new server is a plain list of its tools.
The response is a JSON array, each entry carrying a tool name, a description, and its input schema.
Reading that list first tells you exactly what the server can do before you call anything.
7. Inspecting a Tool Schema
Every tool listing includes an input schema, and reading it saves you from guessing at argument names.
That schema is the same one a client SDK would use to validate arguments before sending them.
8. Calling a Tool with Arguments
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450488-699276105.png
Once you know a tool name and its schema, calling it takes one more command with the arguments attached.

code.content:
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js \
  --method tools/call \
  --tool-name search_notes \
  --tool-arg query=vacation \
  --tool-arg limit=5

blocks.text: Each argument is passed as its own flag, and the tool assembles them into the JSON object the server expects.

blocks.title: Check types before calling
blocks.content: A number argument sent as a bare string can fail validation. Match the schema types exactly.

blocks.text: 9. Reading a Resource
Resources use a different method name, and instead of arguments you pass the resource URI.
The response contains a contents array, usually plain text for a simple resource like this one.
10. Listing and Using Prompts
Prompts follow the same shape, a list method and a get method that takes any parameters the prompt defines.

code.content:
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method prompts/list

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js \
  --method prompts/get --prompt-name summarize_note --prompt-arg noteId=42

blocks.text: The result is a list of messages, exactly what a host would feed into a conversation.
11. Formatting Output with JSON and jq

blocks.alt: Formatting Output with JSON and jq
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450489-412187117.png
Raw JSON output is easy for a script to consume but noisy to read by eye, so piping it through jq helps a lot.
Filtering down to just the names, or just one field of a response, turns a wall of JSON into a short readable line.
12. Config Files and Environment Variables
A server that needs an API key or a database URL still needs those values when launched from a CLI tool.

code.content:
# pass environment variables straight through to the spawned server
API_KEY=abc123 npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method tools/list

# or keep them in a .env file the server itself loads on startup

items: Never hardcode a secret into a CLI command you might paste into chat or a shared terminal
Prefer a local .env file loaded by the server over inline environment variables
Keep a separate config for a staging server versus a production one

blocks.text: 13. Writing a Smoke Test Script
A smoke test is a short script that calls a few tools and checks the server did not fall over.
Nothing fancy here, just grep checks and an exit code, but that is enough to catch a broken server fast.
14. Running Smoke Tests in CI
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450489-22819504.png
The same script that runs on your laptop can run in a CI pipeline with no changes at all.

code.content:
# .github/workflows/mcp-smoke-test.yml
- name: MCP smoke test
  run: |
    npm install
    npm run build
    bash scripts/mcp-smoke-test.sh

blocks.text: A failing exit code fails the build, which catches a broken tool before it ever reaches a real client.
15. CLI vs Full Client: When to Choose Which

blocks.alt: CLI vs Full Client: When to Choose Which
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450489-503939143.png
A CLI is the right tool when the task is a check, not a product.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Better fit"],"rows":[["Quick check a new server works","CLI"],["Smoke test in a CI pipeline","CLI"],["One off exploration of tools and resources","CLI"],["Chat application end users interact with","Full client"],["Custom UI showing tool results visually","Full client"],["Long running agent orchestrating many tool calls","Full client"]]}

blocks.text: If you find yourself scripting the same CLI calls in a loop with real logic around them, that is usually a sign you have outgrown the CLI.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content: Reach for a CLI to check a server. Reach for an SDK client to build something on top of it.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Say you just finished a notes server and want to confirm it works before wiring it into a host.

code.content:
# 1. list tools
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method tools/list

# 2. call add_task with an argument
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js \
  --method tools/call --tool-name add_task --tool-arg title="Buy milk"

# 3. read the resource that should now show the new task
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js \
  --method resources/read --uri tasks://all

blocks.text: Three commands, no client code, and you already know the server behaves correctly end to end.

code.content:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method tools/call \
  --tool-name add_task --tool-arg title="Buy milk" > /tmp/add.json
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method resources/read \
  --uri tasks://all | grep -q "Buy milk" && echo "task server smoke test passed"

blocks.text: Wrap those same three calls in a script, and the manual check becomes a repeatable smoke test.
Common Mistakes

items: Guessing an argument name instead of reading the tool schema first
Forgetting quotes around an argument value that contains spaces
Leaving a secret exposed in plain text inside a CLI command in a shared shell history
Treating a CLI smoke test as a substitute for real client testing before shipping
Not checking the exit code of a CLI call inside a script, letting a silent failure pass
Building an entire product feature by chaining CLI calls instead of switching to an SDK client

blocks.text: Practice
Take any server you already have running and write a three line smoke test script for it.

code.content:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node dist/index.js --method tools/list | grep -q "your_tool_name"
echo "tool found, smoke test passed"

blocks.text: Then add a second check that calls the tool with a real argument and greps the response for expected text.
Key Takeaway
A CLI tool gives you tools/list, tools/call, and resources/read straight from a terminal, no client code required.
Use it to explore a server and to write fast smoke tests, but switch to a real SDK client once you are building something users will actually touch.
